job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Lena Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Lena, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room in Rivergate with my friend Pia, and two other people live in the other room, so there's always someone making pasta. I'm up at seven, I have a coffee, and I check my inbox for replies. Then I work on posts for two cafes and a yoga studio, which I write with an AI tool and then fix by hand, and they pay me about four hundred a month between them. I studied marketing and passed, with no internship, so I've been applying to junior marketing and sales-support roles for five months. I like trying new tools, so my afternoons are usually a mix of job forms and small experiments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected. Useful for first drafts, not magic. I'd tell friends to use it for boring bits and keep the human parts human. Online I'd probably post a cheeky thread about prompts that don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel fine about the tools but not about my own position. I'm a pass-degree graduate with no placement and a small loan, so even in a flat world my CV is thin. My freelance gigs help but they're only four hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd chase more clients, three new small businesses by spring, and make a simple package of posts, a newsletter and a monthly report. I'd keep applying to ten roles a week and mention the freelance work as proof. I'd also join a local marketing meetup and bring a notebook to talk to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit restless. Not scared, just wanting to get on with it, like waiting for a train that's late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do the cafe owners react when you tell them you use AI for the posts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most are fine as long as the posts sound like the cafe. One owner asked me to stop using it, then looked at the engagement numbers and told me to carry on. I think people care about results more than process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first experiment you'd try in a flat world like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tiny shop-sales dashboard, probably. I'd track which posts bring people in and show the cafe owner a chart each month. Owners love a chart with their name on it.

Online I'd post a cheeky thread on **prompts** that don't work.

do: Win **three new** small clients by spring with a posts, newsletter and report package.
Apply to ten roles a week and join a **marketing meetup**.

Keep writing for the two cafes and the yoga studio

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and fast. I'd tell friends to learn the tools now and share what works. Online I'd talk about using AI to do more, not to replace the people who care about the brand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the junior marketing job I'm applying for is exactly what shrinks: drafting copy, scheduling posts, basic reporting. A firm that needed three juniors may need one. I'm better placed than most, but there will be fewer seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn my freelance work into a small business, with a proper name, invoices and a website, and charge per month. I'd learn one more skill each quarter, like video editing or analytics, and aim for a hybrid role at an agency that wants people good with tools. I'd keep a three-month cushion in savings, so I'm not forced into the first offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert and a bit excited. It's like the ground is moving but I'm already on my toes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a junior marketing job get taken first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drafting copy, scheduling, first-pass reports and keyword research. The software does these in minutes. What's left is deciding what the brand should say and being the voice on a call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be afraid of competing against other graduates who use the tools better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. Some of them are very good, and some have the internships I didn't get. That's why I'd rather build my own thing than fight for the same two seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need serious public action now. I'm not extreme about it, but two years isn't time for markets to fix things. I'd say people should help each other, share what they learn and push for support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm unsettled. If AI can do any thinking work as well and cheaper, then my freelancing customers could do it themselves, and my edge vanishes. I'm good with the tools, but so is everyone in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go where a person is needed in the room: events, local business relationships and in-person sales, which are harder to copy early on. I'd keep the cafes as clients, because the owners trust me. I'd cut spending, build a six-month cushion and apply for anything with a licence or a physical presence. I'd ask Pia and the flatmates if we can pool resources if someone loses work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wobbly, honestly. I'd be doing a lot of fast thinking, and not sleeping well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI does the marketing work better and cheaper, what is left for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic, I'm okay, and I'm talking to people. They live in a town where my dad runs a small printing shop, so he'd say come home if it gets bad. I'd probably say yes, with a bit of pride swallowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents, who live far away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to stay useful in ways people can see. A cafe owner who knows me by name is harder to replace than a stranger with a better tool.

I'd tell people to share what they learn and **help** each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to adjust if we get started, so push for training and for a say in how the tools are used. I'd tell friends to build skills that stack: tools, people and a niche.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel cautious but optimistic. I could land a job, grow my freelance base and have options by 2031. I'd still be uncertain about what's left after, but five years of experience is a decent head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first marketing or operations job that pays rent, and keep freelancing on weekends. I'd pick a niche, like local food and drink, where I know the owners. I'd save a third of my income and learn one more skill each half-year, and I'd try to build something that earns without me, like a small paid newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful with some nerves. It feels like a challenge I can actually work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at what clients complained about and what I enjoyed. If three owners say they can't track their numbers, I'd learn analytics. I'd let the market choose, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pick which skill to learn first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me make mistakes. Two years doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. I'd say let's agree on rules, training and fair sharing while there's no emergency. I'd tell friends to stay curious and try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel pretty good. A decade is enough to build a career, start a small company, even change fields if I want to. I'd still keep my eyes open, but I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in an agency for two years, then start my own studio or join a start-up. I'd save for a flat, learn the new tools as they come out, and maybe study part time for a master's in data or business. I'd also volunteer to mentor a younger graduate, because explaining things makes me better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Light, even. It feels like the start of something, not the end of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years feel like a good thing for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something bigger than freelancing. A product maybe, a tool that helps small cafes plan their month. I'd test it with the owners I know, fail small, and try again. With two years I couldn't afford to fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try that you wouldn't try with a shorter timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I'd treat each year as a try-out, and keep a list of what worked.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. Everything I'm good at gets cheaper at once, and I'd have no time to build a base. What would help is public support while people retrain, access to the tools for everyone, and some way to own part of what AI makes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that my generation isn't scared of tools. We're scared of being locked out of the rooms where decisions are made. I'd like to be in those rooms.

portrait: Lena is a 23-year-old marketing graduate who shares a rented room in **Rivergate** and uses AI daily.

She is centrist and adaptive: she treats change as an **experiment** and builds a client base.
She stays uneasy in most pictures, becomes **anxious** at the 2-year warning and calm with ten years.
Her fallback is her father's printing shop, but she would rather build her own thing.
biggestWorry: She worries most about **AGI by 2028**, because everything she is good at gets cheaper at once.
